General Reference

The SEO Field
Overview

Everything that connects the four disciplines — how search engines work, what signals they measure, how quality is judged, and what the research actually says about rankings. Read this before going into any handbook.

6 sections · Full ranking factor table · How Google works · E-E-A-T in depth · 2025 landscape

Section 01

How Google Works — The Full Picture

Google's system operates in three sequential phases. Understanding each phase tells you exactly where an SEO problem is originating — which is the difference between diagnosing it correctly and guessing.

01

Crawling

Googlebot is a fleet of web crawlers that discovers URLs through three mechanisms: links from already-crawled pages, XML sitemaps submitted through Search Console, and direct URL submissions. Googlebot visits each URL, downloads the raw HTML, and queues it for rendering.

Crawl budget — the number of pages Google will crawl on your site within a given period — is finite and allocated by domain authority and server response time. Wasting it on paginated archives, filtered URLs, or thin parameter pages means important content gets crawled less frequently. Crawl problems are invisible to users but catastrophic to SEO.

02

Rendering

After crawling, Google processes pages through its Web Rendering Service — a headless Chromium instance that executes JavaScript. This step matters enormously for modern frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) where content is injected by JavaScript rather than present in the raw HTML.

Rendering is queued separately from crawling and can happen hours or days later. Content that only exists post-JavaScript-execution may not be indexed reliably. This is why server-side rendering (SSR) or static generation is strongly preferred for SEO-critical content.

03

Indexing

Rendered pages are analysed for content, structure, and quality signals, then stored in Google's index — a distributed database of trillions of documents. Not every crawled page gets indexed. Thin content, duplicate content, soft 404s, and noindex directives all result in pages being excluded.

The Coverage report in Google Search Console is your primary diagnostic: it shows exactly which pages are indexed, which are excluded, and why. Regularly auditing this report is a non-negotiable habit for anyone doing serious SEO.

04

Ranking

When a user submits a query, Google retrieves matching documents from the index and runs them through a layered ranking system. The system includes hundreds of signals, several machine learning models (including the BERT and MUM language models), and human quality rater feedback that trains the systems over time.

Ranking signals are weighted differently by query type and competitive landscape. A local search for "best pizza near me" weights proximity, review volume, and GBP completeness heavily. A YMYL (Your Money, Your Life) query about a medical condition weights E-E-A-T signals far above typical content signals.

05

SERP Features

Modern SERPs contain far more than ten blue links. Featured Snippets, People Also Ask boxes, Knowledge Panels, Local Packs, Shopping carousels, Image packs, Video results, and AI Overviews all compete for screen real estate above traditional organic listings.

This matters strategically: 58% of searches now end without a click — Google answers the query directly in the SERP. Optimising for Featured Snippets and structured data rich results is increasingly important not just for rankings but for visibility in a zero-click environment.

"Most SEO failures are not content failures — they are technical failures that prevent great content from ever being seen."

Section 02

The Four Pillars — In Depth

The four pillars are not equally weighted in every context. A brand-new site needs technical foundations before anything else. A content-heavy site competing in an established niche needs off-page authority. Understanding where each pillar has highest leverage — and in what sequence — is the core strategic skill of SEO.

Pillar 01 — Technical 01

Technical SEO

Technical SEO is the infrastructure layer. It ensures that search engine crawlers can discover, access, render, and understand every page that matters. When technical SEO fails, even the best content on the internet cannot rank — because Google may never see it, or may see a broken version of it.

The discipline covers: crawlability (robots.txt, noindex, crawl budget), indexability (canonical tags, duplicate content, hreflang), renderability (JavaScript execution, server-side vs client-side rendering), page speed (Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS), mobile usability (mobile-first indexing since 2023), structured data (Schema.org markup for rich results), and site architecture (URL structure, internal linking, sitemaps).

Technical audits should be run on a regular cadence — not just when something breaks. A quarterly crawl with Screaming Frog, a monthly review of Search Console's Coverage and Experience reports, and continuous Core Web Vitals monitoring are the minimum practice for any site doing serious SEO work.

Pillar 02 — On-Page 02

Content & On-Page SEO

On-page SEO is the relevance layer. It is where you communicate to Google what each page is about, and where you match your content to what users actually need when they submit a query. This is the discipline most content writers touch directly — and the one most frequently misunderstood.

The foundational concept is search intent: the underlying goal behind a query. A user searching "how to fix a slow website" has informational intent — they want to learn. A user searching "buy SSL certificate" has transactional intent — they want to purchase. A page that answers the wrong intent will not rank, regardless of how well-written the content is.

On-page factors in priority order: title tag (the highest-impact single element on any page), meta description (CTR signal, not a ranking factor directly), H1 (one per page, should match or be close to the title tag), heading hierarchy (H2–H4 for structure and secondary keyword coverage), body content (depth, originality, and accuracy — not word count alone), internal linking (PageRank distribution and topical authority building), image alt text, and URL structure.

→ Open Content Writer's Handbook — 11 Chapters
Pillar 03 — Off-Page 03

Off-Page & Link Building

Off-page SEO is the authority layer. It consists of signals that exist outside your own site but tell Google how the broader web perceives your content. The primary off-page signal is backlinks — links from other websites to yours. The original insight behind PageRank (Google's foundational algorithm) was that a link from one site to another is essentially a vote of confidence.

Not all links are equal. A single contextual link from a high-authority, topically relevant publication is worth more than hundreds of low-quality directory links. The key metrics for evaluating link quality are Domain Rating or Domain Authority (the estimated authority of the linking domain), topical relevance (does the linking site cover the same subject matter?), link placement (in-content links are weighted more than sidebar or footer links), and anchor text (the clickable text of the link, which signals relevance).

The sustainable approach to link building is creating content that deserves links — original research, comprehensive tools, data studies, and definitive guides. This is complemented by proactive outreach: digital PR campaigns, expert commentary, guest posts on relevant publications, and broken link reclamation. What does not work in 2025: link schemes, paid links disguised as editorial, private blog networks (PBNs), and automated link building.

→ Open Link Building Handbook — 11 Chapters
Pillar 04 — Local / E-E-A-T 04

Local SEO & E-E-A-T

Local SEO and E-E-A-T are both expressions of the same underlying principle: trustworthiness is a ranking signal. Google's systems have become increasingly capable of distinguishing genuine expertise from manufactured credibility, and penalising sites that attempt to fake it.

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. It is the framework Google's quality raters use to evaluate pages — particularly for YMYL (Your Money, Your Life) content covering health, finance, legal, and safety topics. Building E-E-A-T means: credentialed authors with transparent bios, first-hand experience demonstrated in the content itself, citations from external authoritative sources, an accurate and complete About page, and consistent brand presence across the web.

Local SEO applies these trust principles to geographic context. The Local Pack (the map and three business listings that appear for location-based queries) is governed primarily by: Google Business Profile completeness and activity, proximity to the searcher, review volume and sentiment, NAP (Name, Address, Phone) consistency across all online directories, and local backlinks from regionally relevant sites.

Section 03

The Ranking Factor Landscape

Google has never published a complete list of ranking factors. What follows is compiled from official Google documentation, confirmed statements from Google engineers, large-scale ranking correlation studies, and the known effects of algorithm updates. Treat impact levels as directional — the right answer always depends on the specific query, niche, and competitive landscape.

Factor Pillar Impact Notes
Content relevance and depth On-Page Critical Must comprehensively match search intent. Not about word count — about thoroughness relative to competing pages.
Backlink quality and quantity Off-Page Critical Primary authority signal. Weight varies by niche — competitive queries require significantly stronger link profiles.
Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) Technical High Confirmed ranking signal since 2021. INP replaced FID in 2024. Sites failing thresholds face measurable ranking suppression.
E-E-A-T signals Trust High Especially critical for YMYL content. Author credentials, external citations, brand mentions across trusted domains.
Mobile usability Technical High Mobile-first indexing is the default since 2023. Google indexes the mobile version of your site, not the desktop version.
Keyword in title tag On-Page High The single highest-impact on-page element. Front-loading the target keyword in the title has a measurable effect on rankings.
Internal linking structure Technical / On-Page Medium–High Distributes PageRank. Communicates topical authority. Orphan pages (no internal links) rank poorly regardless of quality.
Structured data / Schema Technical Medium Not a direct ranking factor, but enables rich results that significantly lift CTR. FAQ, HowTo, Product, and Review schema have the most SERP impact.
Page speed (TTFB, overall load) Technical Medium Overlaps with Core Web Vitals. Slow servers harm both ranking and user experience metrics simultaneously.
HTTPS / security Technical Medium Confirmed ranking signal since 2014. In 2025 it is effectively table stakes — any site without HTTPS is penalised implicitly.
Keyword in H1 and subheadings On-Page Medium H1 should match or closely mirror the title tag. H2–H4 headings covering semantic variants aid topical coverage assessment.
Content freshness On-Page Medium Query-dependent. High for news and trending topics, low for evergreen how-to content. Refresh dates on updated content signal recency.
Dwell time and engagement On-Page Medium (indirect) Google denies using GA data. However, user engagement signals from Chrome and Search are likely inputs. Thin, unsatisfying content produces visible bounce signals.
Domain age and history Off-Page Low–Medium Older domains with clean histories have a trust baseline advantage. Not a substitute for quality signals — but a new domain faces a trust deficit.
Exact-match anchor text of incoming links Off-Page Medium (high risk) Still influential, but a profile dominated by exact-match anchors triggers Penguin-era spam filters. Branded and natural anchors should dominate.
Social signals Off-Page Indirect Google has confirmed social links are not direct ranking signals. High-performing social content correlates with earned backlinks — the real benefit.
Keyword density On-Page Myth / Harmful Not a ranking factor. Optimising for keyword density produces unnatural writing that modern NLP systems penalise. Focus on topical coverage instead.
Meta keywords tag On-Page Ignored Google has not used the meta keywords tag since 2009. It is irrelevant — though it cannot harm rankings either.

Section 04

Algorithm Evolution — What Changed and Why

Every major Google update represents a shift in what the algorithm measures or how it weighs signals. Understanding the trajectory of these updates explains why certain tactics stop working and what the next generation of SEO demands.

2011

Panda — Content Quality

Targeted thin, duplicate, and low-quality content. Introduced the concept of site-wide quality assessment — one cluster of bad pages could suppress an entire domain's rankings. Killed content farms and article spinners.

2012

Penguin — Link Manipulation

Targeted manipulative backlink profiles — paid links, link schemes, and exact-match anchor text overuse. Became real-time in 2016, meaning toxic link cleanup now affects rankings immediately upon recrawl rather than waiting for the next update.

2013

Hummingbird — Semantic Search

Replaced keyword-matching logic with semantic understanding of queries. Google began understanding the intent behind a search, not just the literal words. Made keyword-stuffing irrelevant and elevated the importance of topical authority.

2019

BERT — Natural Language Processing

Applied transformer-based language models to query understanding. Google could now understand context, nuance, and the relationship between words in a query. Particularly impactful on long-tail and conversational queries. Writing naturally for humans became more effective than writing for keyword patterns.

2022–23

Helpful Content System

Introduced a site-wide quality classifier targeting content written primarily for search engines rather than people. Sites with high proportions of unhelpful, AI-generated, or aggregated-without-value content saw broad ranking drops. The update elevated original research, first-hand experience, and genuine expertise above all other content signals.

2024–25

AI Overviews — The Zero-Click Era

Google's AI-generated summary responses, appearing above organic results, now answer a significant share of informational queries directly in the SERP. The implication: informational content that previously drove traffic increasingly does not — but the pages cited in AI Overviews gain brand authority and indirect traffic. Optimising for citation in AI summaries is an emerging discipline.

Section 05

The SEO Tool Ecosystem

No single tool does everything. Professional SEO practice involves a core stack of complementary tools, each measuring a different layer of the system. Here is what each tool category covers and the leading options in each.

Category What it measures Leading tools Cost
Search console Impressions, clicks, position, index coverage, Core Web Vitals, manual actions Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools Free
Traffic analytics Sessions, users, engagement, channel attribution, conversions Google Analytics 4 Free
All-in-one SEO platform Rankings, backlinks, keyword research, site audit, competitor analysis Ahrefs, Semrush, Moz Pro $99–$499/mo
Technical site crawling Broken links, redirect chains, duplicate content, meta issues, crawl depth Screaming Frog SEO Spider, Sitebulb Free tier / £149/yr
Page speed / Core Web Vitals LCP, INP, CLS, TTFB, field data vs lab data PageSpeed Insights, WebPageTest, Lighthouse Free
Keyword research Search volume, keyword difficulty, SERP features, related queries Ahrefs Keywords Explorer, Semrush Keyword Magic, Google Keyword Planner Free–$129/mo
Local SEO Local pack rankings, GBP performance, citation tracking BrightLocal, Whitespark, Local Falcon $29–$79/mo
Schema / structured data Schema validation, rich result eligibility testing Google Rich Results Test, Schema Markup Validator Free
Rank tracking Daily keyword position tracking across locations and devices STAT, Advanced Web Ranking, SerpWatcher $29–$720/mo
Log file analysis Googlebot crawl behaviour from server logs Screaming Frog Log Analyser, Splunk, custom scripts Free–enterprise

The minimum viable stack for most practitioners: Google Search Console + GA4 (both free) + one all-in-one platform (Ahrefs or Semrush) + Screaming Frog for technical audits. Everything else is additive.
